key_points: Detection engineering turns attacker behavior into durable, testable logic.
MITRE ATT&CK is the shared map: tactics (why) and techniques (how).
Sigma/YARA-style rules encode hypotheses; tuning is a measurement discipline.
Every detection needs a validation story: emulate the technique, verify the alert.
domains.name: Detection Engineer Track

choices: Map it to Exfiltration -- PowerShell always means data theft
Map it to Execution (T1059.001) -- the technique describes how code runs, regardless of the end goal
Map it to Defense Evasion -- obfuscation is the whole story
Do not map it -- encoded commands are too generic to classify
evidence: EDR fired on powershell.exe -EncodedCommand <base64> spawning from a Word macro on FIN-WS-114.
The same pattern preceded credential dumping in last month's incident.
scenarios.hint: Tactics describe the attacker's objective; techniques describe the method. Which one is stable here?
scenarios.prompt: How should this detection be mapped in ATT&CK?
scenarios.situation: You are writing a detection for encoded PowerShell launched from Office macros. The rule fires, and now you need the ATT&CK mapping for the runbook, the coverage map, and the purple-team test plan.
scenarios.title: Mapping the encoded launcher
scenarios.why: T1059.001 (PowerShell) under the Execution tactic is the stable mapping: the technique describes the mechanism (running code via PowerShell), which stays constant whether the objective is dumping credentials, establishing persistence, or exfiltrating. Mapping to the end goal (Exfiltration, Credential Access) would splinter one detection into many and break your coverage map every time the attacker changes objectives.

choices: selection: Image|endswith: powershell.exe AND CommandLine|contains: EncodedCommand; condition: selection
selection: Image|endswith: 'powershell.exe', ParentImage|endswith: ['winword.exe','excel.exe'], CommandLine|contains: '-EncodedCommand'; condition: selection
selection: Image: '*powershell*'; condition: selection -- broad is better
selection: CommandLine|contains: 'mimikatz'; condition: selection
evidence: Process creation logs carry Image, ParentImage, CommandLine for every launch.
powershell.exe runs thousands of times daily from admin scripts, SCCM, and logon tasks.
scenarios.hint: Precision comes from combining fields. Which combination separates macro-launched from admin-launched?
scenarios.prompt: Which rule logic best detects the malicious pattern without drowning the SOC?
scenarios.situation: You need a Sigma-style rule for encoded PowerShell spawned by Office applications. Raw powershell.exe executions number in the thousands per day; the malicious pattern is a thin slice.
scenarios.title: Writing the Sigma logic
scenarios.why: Detection quality is a logic problem, not a volume problem. Combining three fields -- the interpreter, the suspicious argument, and the unusual parent -- isolates the malicious slice from the thousands of benign admin executions. The broad rule would fire constantly and get disabled; the mimikatz-only rule misses every other payload. Conjunction across fields is how you buy precision without losing recall.

choices: Tune it: add exclusions for the known-benign updater paths, set a per-host throttle, and measure the false-positive rate for a week before promoting to blocking
Disable the rule -- noisy rules are worse than no rules
Promote to blocking immediately -- a noisy block is better than a quiet miss
Rewrite it to match only the exact hash from the incident
evidence: Rule 'suspicious rundll32' fired 412 times last week; analyst review found 3 true positives, all the same red-team exercise.
Legitimate software updaters use rundll32 with unusual arguments across 800 hosts.
scenarios.hint: The rule has signal (3 real hits) buried in noise. What preserves the signal while killing the noise?
scenarios.prompt: The rule works but it is noisy. What is the right tuning move?
scenarios.situation: Your rundll32 detection caught real red-team activity -- but also fired 409 false positives from legitimate updaters. The SOC lead wants it either fixed or gone by Friday.
scenarios.title: Taming the noisy rule
scenarios.why: Disabling loses the 3 true positives; blocking on noise trains everyone to ignore the rule; hash-matching collapses coverage to one sample. Tuning is measurement-driven: exclude the known-benign updater paths, throttle per-host repetition, then measure the false-positive rate over a week. A rule graduates to blocking only when its precision earns analyst trust.

choices: Escalate immediately -- encoded PowerShell is always malicious
Enrich first: check parent process, user, host role, and whether this admin runs such scripts routinely -- then decide
Close as benign -- admins use PowerShell constantly
Isolate the host before any investigation -- speed beats context
evidence: powershell.exe -EncodedCommand on SRV-BACKUP-02, user: backup-admin, parent: legitimate backup scheduler.
backup-admin runs encoded commands nightly; the strings decode to backup rotation logic.
scenarios.hint: The same telemetry, two different stories. What distinguishes them?
scenarios.prompt: How should the analyst triage this alert?
scenarios.situation: Your new encoded-PowerShell rule fires on SRV-BACKUP-02: backup-admin's account, parent is the legitimate backup scheduler, and the decoded strings are backup rotation logic the admin runs nightly.
scenarios.title: True positive or busy admin?
scenarios.why: Triage is context application, not reflex. Parent process (legitimate scheduler), user (backup-admin), host role (backup server), and historical pattern (nightly, decoded content benign) all point to a true negative -- but one worth documenting as a tuning candidate (exclude this scheduler path) rather than a silent close. Escalating or isolating on every encoded-command alert would burn the SOC's credibility within a week.

choices: Write a hash blocklist for each LOLBins binary -- hashes are precise
Block the LOLBins binaries entirely -- nobody needs them
Build behavior-based rules on LOLBins invocation patterns (parent, arguments, network) because the binaries are legitimate and irreplaceable
Ignore LOLBins -- allowlisted binaries cannot be malicious
evidence: Attackers used mshta.exe, rundll32.exe, and certutil.exe in 4 of the last 6 incidents. All are signed Microsoft binaries.
IT uses the same binaries for software deployment; blocking them breaks patching.
scenarios.hint: The binary is innocent. What is guilty?
scenarios.prompt: How do you get detection coverage on living-off-the-land binaries?
scenarios.situation: Signed Microsoft binaries -- mshta, rundll32, certutil -- featured in 4 of your last 6 incidents. They are also essential to IT's patching workflow, so blocking or hash-listing them is off the table.
scenarios.title: The LOLBins gap
scenarios.why: Living-off-the-land binaries are trusted by signature and needed by IT, so identity-based controls fail twice. Coverage comes from behavior: unusual parents, suspicious arguments (javascript:, -urlcache), and network connections from binaries that should never phone home. Behavior rules distinguish the attacker's mshta from IT's mshta -- the binary name was never the signal.

choices: Process-creation plus LSASS-access telemetry (Sysmon/EDR): which process opened lsass.exe and with what access mask
Firewall logs alone -- network is the only ground truth
Email gateway logs -- credential theft starts with phishing
DNS logs alone -- every attack needs DNS
evidence: Attacker dumps credentials via comsvcs.dll MiniDump or direct LSASS handle access.
EDR records process creation with command lines and LSASS access events with granted access masks.
scenarios.hint: Credential dumping is a process-memory operation. Which sensor sees process memory access?
scenarios.prompt: Which telemetry best detects credential dumping?
scenarios.situation: You are building detection for credential dumping (LSASS access via comsvcs MiniDump and direct handle opens). You must pick the primary log source to build on.
scenarios.title: Which telemetry for credential dumping?
scenarios.why: Match the sensor to the mechanism: dumping is a process opening LSASS with memory-read rights, so process-creation plus LSASS-access telemetry with access masks is the direct observation. Comsvcs MiniDump has a distinctive command line; direct opens show as specific access masks. Network, email, and DNS logs see at best side effects -- build primary detection on the sensor that watches the act itself.

choices: Alert on the hash -- IOCs are the detection
Alert on the IP -- infrastructure is stable
Hunt the TTPs (technique patterns) across the estate -- behaviors outlive indicators
Wait for the vendor to publish a signature
evidence: New ransomware affiliate: uses BITSAdmin for download, WMI for persistence, vssadmin to delete shadow copies. Hashes and IPs rotate per victim.
You have Sysmon + EDR on 90% of hosts with 90-day retention.
scenarios.hint: What survives per-victim rotation of hashes and IPs?
scenarios.prompt: Intel gives you rotating IOCs and stable TTPs. What do you operationalize?
scenarios.situation: Threat intel describes a new ransomware affiliate: BITSAdmin downloads, WMI persistence, vssadmin shadow-copy deletion. Hashes and IPs rotate per victim. You have broad EDR telemetry with 90-day retention.
scenarios.title: From intel to detection
scenarios.why: IOCs are per-victim disposable; the affiliate rotates them deliberately. TTPs -- the how -- are expensive to change and stable across victims. Operationalize behavior: BITSAdmin-to-suspicious-URL, WMI event subscription creation, vssadmin delete shadows as a correlated sequence. Hunt the TTPs retroactively across 90 days of telemetry; alert on hashes and you will always be one victim behind.

choices: Trust the vendor datasheet -- it claims coverage
Write the rule and ship it -- code review is the validation
Emulate the technique in a test environment and verify the alert fires with correct severity and context -- untested detections are assumed absent
Ask the SOC if they have seen it -- absence of alerts proves coverage
evidence: Detects LSASS dumping via comsvcs.dll MiniDump -- written, peer-reviewed, not yet tested.
Last quarter, an untested rule silently failed to fire during a real incident (broken field name).
scenarios.hint: What is the difference between a rule that exists and a detection that works?
scenarios.prompt: The rule is written and reviewed. What proves it works?
scenarios.situation: Your comsvcs MiniDump rule is written and peer-reviewed. Last quarter, an untested rule with a broken field name silently failed during a real incident. The CISO asks for proof of coverage.
scenarios.title: Purple-team validation
scenarios.why: A rule that has never fired on a real technique is a hypothesis, not a control. Validation means emulating the technique (atomic red-team style) in a test environment and confirming the alert fires with the right severity, fields, and runbook link. Datasheets claim, code review checks logic, but only emulation proves the full pipeline -- sensor, rule, alert, queue -- actually works.

choices: Cover every technique equally -- completeness is the goal
Cover the techniques in the news -- visibility matters
Prioritize coverage by risk: techniques targeting your crown jewels and seen in your threat landscape first; document the rest as accepted gaps
Only cover techniques you have already been hit by
evidence: 47% of ATT&CK techniques have a mapped detection; adversary intel says your sector is hit with valid-account abuse and encrypted C2.
scenarios.hint: You cannot cover everything. What orders the work?
scenarios.prompt: 47% technique coverage, two engineers, one quarter. How do you prioritize?
scenarios.situation: Your ATT&CK coverage map shows 47% of techniques with mapped detections. Threat intel says your sector faces valid-account abuse and encrypted C2. You have two detection engineers for the quarter.
scenarios.title: The coverage map
scenarios.why: Coverage is a risk decision, not a completeness exercise. Prioritize techniques that threaten your crown jewels and appear in your threat landscape -- valid-account abuse and encrypted C2 here -- then document remaining gaps as explicit accepted risks with compensating controls. Equal coverage spreads two engineers across trivia; news-driven coverage chases headlines; incident-only coverage learns exclusively from failure.

key_points: Solutions engineers translate Zero Trust into business risk and operational reality.
Demos must be honest: show the policy working, including the approval workflow.
Objection handling: differentiate default-deny from detection-based tools.
Troubleshooting follows scope: policy, agent, inheritance, version.
domains.name: Solutions Engineer Track

choices: Explain kernel hooks and driver architecture in depth -- technical buyers respect depth
Frame it in business risk: ransomware cannot run what is never approved; translate blocks into incidents prevented and downtime avoided
Promise zero false positives -- confidence closes deals
Focus on the dashboard's color scheme -- executives buy UX
evidence: CFO, 30-minute slot, no security background. Previous vendor lost her on 'heuristic entropy analysis'.
She signs off on the budget if the risk reduction is concrete.
scenarios.hint: She buys risk reduction, not technology. What is the one-sentence business case?
scenarios.prompt: How do you explain allowlisting to a CFO in 30 minutes?
scenarios.situation: You have 30 minutes with a CFO who controls the security budget. She has no security background and tuned out the last vendor's deep technical dive. You need her to fund a default-deny endpoint project.
scenarios.title: Explain allowlisting to a CFO
scenarios.why: Executives buy outcomes: ransomware that cannot execute, incidents that never start, downtime avoided. Translate the mechanism once ('only approved software runs; everything else is stopped by default') then spend the slot on her risks -- cost of a breach, cost of downtime, audit findings closed. Technical depth is for the follow-up with her engineers; promising zero false positives destroys credibility the first week.

choices: Blame the customer's environment -- demos never fail on your side
Disable the agent and continue the demo -- the show must go on
Acknowledge it, pivot to the approval workflow: show how the block becomes a request, an approval, and a policy -- the product working as designed
End the demo early -- a failed demo cannot be saved
evidence: Live demo: agent blocks the prospect's line-of-business app mid-presentation. Room goes quiet.
The app was never submitted through the Testing Environment approval flow before the demo.
scenarios.hint: The product did exactly what it is supposed to do. What story does that tell?
scenarios.prompt: The agent blocks the prospect's app live in the demo. What do you do?
scenarios.situation: Mid-demo, the endpoint agent blocks the prospect's line-of-business application. The room goes quiet. The app was never run through the approval workflow before the demo.
scenarios.title: Demo gone wrong
scenarios.why: The block is the product working -- denying unknown software by default is the entire value proposition. The recovery is to narrate it: show the block event, submit the approval request, approve it through the workflow, and relaunch the app. You just demonstrated prevention plus the operational process in one unplanned moment. Disabling the agent would demonstrate that your security evaporates under pressure.

choices: Differentiate the model: antivirus asks 'is this known-bad?' (default-allow); allowlisting asks 'is this known-good?' (default-deny) -- unknown ransomware runs on AV, stops on default-deny
Agree that AV is enough -- avoid conflict
Claim AV never works -- FUD wins deals
Pivot to pricing -- cost is the real objection
evidence: 'We already pay for antivirus. Why do we need this?' -- IT director, 200 endpoints.
The prospect had a ransomware incident last year via an unsigned payload their AV did not recognize.
scenarios.hint: Their own incident is the answer. What did the AV do about the unknown payload?
scenarios.prompt: 'We already have antivirus.' What is the honest differentiator?
scenarios.situation: An IT director with 200 endpoints objects: they already pay for antivirus. Last year they suffered a ransomware incident from an unsigned payload their AV did not recognize.
scenarios.title: We already have antivirus
scenarios.why: The models are opposites: AV is default-allow with a blocklist (runs everything until proven bad); allowlisting is default-deny (runs only approved software). Their own incident proves the gap -- the unknown payload ran because nothing knew it was bad yet. No FUD needed: name the models, cite their incident, and let the architecture difference do the work.

choices: Reinstall the agent -- agents break constantly
Check policy scope and inheritance, agent version and last check-in, then the policy assignment for the device group
Rebuild the policy from scratch -- faster than debugging
Blame the network -- policies need perfect connectivity
evidence: New USB-control policy applies to 190 of 200 endpoints. 10 show 'policy not received'.
Stale agent versions, devices in the wrong group, inheritance blocked at the OU.
scenarios.hint: Scope, agent, inheritance, version -- in that order.
scenarios.prompt: Policy reached 190 of 200 endpoints. How do you troubleshoot the 10?
scenarios.situation: A new USB-control policy applied to 190 of 200 endpoints. Ten show 'policy not received'. The customer is watching you troubleshoot live.
scenarios.title: Policy not applying
scenarios.why: Troubleshoot in scope order: is the device in the targeted group (scope), is inheritance blocked, is the agent current and checking in (version/last check-in), then the assignment itself. Random reinstallation or rebuilds waste the live session; methodical scope-first diagnosis usually lands on group membership or a stale agent within minutes -- and it demonstrates operational competence to the customer.

choices: Promise the false-positive rate is zero -- confidence reassures
Say false positives are unavoidable -- honesty means fatalism
Explain the controls: Testing Environment for safe approval, granular policy scoping, and the request-approval workflow that turns unknown blocks into 2-minute decisions
Avoid the question -- change the subject to pricing
evidence: 'What about false positives? Our last tool blocked payroll.' -- prospect, burned before.
Default-deny will block unknown good software; the question is how fast the workflow unblocks it.
scenarios.hint: The prospect was burned by blocks with no recourse. What is different here?
scenarios.prompt: 'What about false positives? Our last tool blocked payroll.'
scenarios.situation: A prospect burned by a previous tool that blocked payroll asks about false positives. Default-deny will block unknown legitimate software -- the differentiator is what happens next.
scenarios.title: The false-positive question
scenarios.why: Do not promise zero -- default-deny blocks unknowns by design, including legitimate ones. The honest answer sells the workflow: the Testing Environment for safe vetting, granular scoping so policies fit teams, and the request-approval loop that converts a block into an approved application in minutes. Their old tool failed on recourse, not on blocking; show the recourse.

choices: Explain it as least-privilege for applications: the app runs, but its risky capabilities (network, scripting, spawning children) are stripped -- breach containment
Describe it as antivirus with a new name
Say it encrypts the application
Claim it makes applications run faster
evidence: Prospect asks what Ringfencing actually does, technically, in one minute.
A fenced app can do its job but cannot reach the network, launch scripts, or spawn processes.
scenarios.hint: The app still runs. What can it no longer do?
scenarios.prompt: Explain Ringfencing technically in one minute.
scenarios.situation: The prospect's engineer asks what Ringfencing actually does, technically. You have one minute before the meeting moves on.
scenarios.title: Ringfencing in sixty seconds
scenarios.why: Ringfencing is application least-privilege: the application runs normally, but its dangerous capabilities -- network access, script execution, child processes, registry writes -- are fenced off by policy. A compromised fenced app cannot easily download payloads, move laterally, or persist. One mechanism, one sentence each for what it is, what it stops, and why it matters: containment of the already-running.

choices: Big-bang rollout -- speed impresses
Single-site pilot, then phased waves with success criteria per wave: deployment health, policy stability, approval SLA
Roll out to executives first -- they are the most patient
Deploy everywhere but leave policies in monitor-only forever
evidence: 3 sites, 1,200 endpoints, one IT generalist per site.
A bad policy at full scale blocks all 1,200 at once.
scenarios.hint: What limits the blast radius of a bad policy?
scenarios.prompt: 3 sites, 1,200 endpoints, one IT generalist per site. What is the rollout plan?
scenarios.situation: A 1,200-endpoint, 3-site prospect with one IT generalist per site is ready to buy. A misconfigured policy at full scale would block all 1,200 endpoints simultaneously.
scenarios.title: Multi-site rollout
scenarios.why: Phased rollout with per-wave success criteria: pilot one site (or one department), verify deployment health, policy stability, and approval SLA, then expand in waves. This bounds the blast radius of a bad policy and builds the local generalist's competence before scale. Big-bang optimizes for demo speed and risks a company-wide outage; monitor-only forever never delivers the prevention they bought.

choices: Position prevention-first: their EDR detects after execution; default-deny prevents execution -- different stage of the kill chain, complementary not duplicative
Claim EDR is useless -- displacement wins
Agree it overlaps -- offer a discount to compensate
Avoid the topic -- talk about reporting instead
evidence: Prospect runs a well-tuned EDR with a 24/7 SOC. They ask why they need allowlisting too.
Their EDR caught last year's ransomware -- after it encrypted 30 workstations. Dwell time: 6 hours.
scenarios.hint: Their own incident has two phases: before and after execution. Which did the EDR cover?
scenarios.prompt: Prospect has a good EDR and SOC. Why add allowlisting?
scenarios.situation: A prospect with a well-tuned EDR and 24/7 SOC asks why they need allowlisting. Last year their EDR caught ransomware -- after it encrypted 30 workstations over 6 hours.
scenarios.title: The EDR-only shop
scenarios.why: Different kill-chain stages: EDR detects and responds after execution (their 6-hour dwell time and 30 encrypted hosts prove the cost of post-execution defense); default-deny prevents the execution itself. The honest position is complementary, not duplicative -- prevention shrinks what detection must catch. Claiming EDR is useless insults the team you need as champions.

choices: Number of dashboards viewed -- engagement proves value
Vendor's word that it works -- trust the experts
Block rate on unknown samples, false-positive rate, and mean time-to-approve -- prevention, precision, and operational cost
Lowest price per endpoint -- procurement decides
evidence: The prospect needs a renewal-grade decision at day 30.
scenarios.hint: What would make the CFO renew on day 31?
scenarios.prompt: What three metrics decide the 30-day PoC?
scenarios.situation: A 30-day PoC on 100 endpoints must produce a renewal-grade decision. You get to define the success criteria up front.
scenarios.title: Success metrics for the PoC
scenarios.why: Three metrics cover the buying decision: block rate on unknown samples (does the prevention work), false-positive rate (what does it cost the business), and mean time-to-approve (what does it cost operations). Defined up front, they turn day 30 from an opinion into a measurement. Dashboard views measure curiosity; price measures procurement, not value.

key_points: Pipelines are products: build, test, scan, deploy -- with gates that fail closed.
IaC is code: review it, test it, never apply blind.
Kubernetes troubleshooting: describe, logs, events -- in that order.
Automation must be idempotent, secret-free, and observable.
domains.name: Junior DevOps Engineer Track

choices: Re-run the pipeline -- flakes fix themselves
Read the failed stage's logs, reproduce the failure locally or in a branch, then fix the cause
Delete the pipeline and rebuild it -- faster than debugging
Skip the failing stage -- it is probably not important
evidence: Deploy stage failed: 'image pull backoff' on the new tag.
The image tag referenced in the manifest was never pushed -- the build stage was skipped on this run.
scenarios.hint: The log names the cause. What is the discipline?
scenarios.prompt: Deploy stage fails with image pull backoff. What is the method?
scenarios.situation: Your CI/CD deploy stage fails: the manifest references an image tag that was never pushed because the build stage was skipped on this run.
scenarios.title: Pipeline failure
scenarios.why: Troubleshoot pipelines like systems: read the failed stage's logs first (they named the cause -- missing tag), reproduce in a branch, fix the cause (stage dependency), not the symptom. Re-running flakes, rebuilding blindly, or skipping stages all guarantee the 3 AM recurrence. The log is the diagnosis; the stage graph is the prescription.

choices: Apply it -- plans are usually right
Review the plan line by line, identify why destroy is proposed (renamed resource vs. real deletion), and never apply a surprise destroy
Apply with -auto-approve -- speed matters
Delete the state file -- it is clearly corrupt
evidence: Plan: 3 to add, 1 to destroy. The destroy is the production database.
A resource was renamed in the config last commit; the state still maps the old name.
scenarios.hint: Why would Terraform want to destroy a database you still need?
scenarios.prompt: Terraform plans to destroy the production database. What do you do?
scenarios.situation: Terraform plan shows 3 to add, 1 to destroy -- and the destroy is the production database. A resource was renamed in the last commit; state still maps the old name.
scenarios.title: Terraform wants to destroy prod
scenarios.why: A rename looks like delete-plus-create to Terraform: the plan is honest about its confusion, and applying it destroys the database. The discipline: read every plan, explain every destroy before approving, and fix the cause (state mv for renames) rather than the symptom. Never apply a surprise destroy; never auto-approve production. IaC's power is also its blast radius.

choices: It is fine -- the repo is private
Rotate the secret immediately, purge it from history, move it to a vault, and audit for use
Just delete the file -- the secret is gone
Change the secret next quarter -- it is low priority
evidence: AWS access key committed to the repo 6 months ago, in 40 subsequent commits.
The repo was briefly public last month during a settings change.
scenarios.hint: Who has read that repo in the last 6 months?
scenarios.prompt: An AWS key sat in the repo for 6 months, briefly public. What is the response?
scenarios.situation: An AWS access key was committed 6 months ago, survives in 40 commits of history, and the repo was briefly public last month.
scenarios.title: Secret in the repo
scenarios.why: Treat it as compromised: rotate immediately (the key is burned the moment it touched version control), purge from history (rewritten history, force-push, notify collaborators), move to a vault with rotation, and audit CloudTrail for use. Deleting the file leaves 40 commits of exposure; 'private repo' was already disproven. Secrets in git are incidents, not housekeeping.

choices: kubectl describe, then logs, then events -- find whether it is config, image, or resource pressure
Delete the pod -- Kubernetes heals itself
Scale to 10 replicas -- one will survive
Restart the cluster -- clean slate
evidence: Liveness probe fails: app listens on 8080, probe hits 80.
scenarios.hint: CrashLoopBackOff is a symptom. What does describe say?
scenarios.prompt: Pod in CrashLoopBackOff for 20 minutes. What is the order of operations?
scenarios.situation: A pod has been CrashLoopBackOff for 20 minutes. kubectl describe shows the liveness probe failing: the app listens on 8080, the probe hits port 80.
scenarios.title: CrashLoopBackOff
scenarios.why: Describe, logs, events -- in that order: describe revealed the port mismatch (probe 80 vs. app 8080), the most common CrashLoop cause family (config/probe mismatch). Deleting the pod recreates the same broken config; scaling multiplies it; restarting the cluster is theater. Kubernetes tells you exactly what is wrong if you ask in the right order.

choices: Scripts that work once are fine -- reruns are rare
Make it idempotent: safe to re-run, checks state before acting, no duplicate side effects
Add more logging -- observability replaces safety
Run everything as root -- fewer permission errors
evidence: The user-provisioning script ran twice after a retry; 200 duplicate accounts created.
No existence checks; every run appends.
scenarios.hint: Retries happen. What should the second run do?
scenarios.prompt: A retry created 200 duplicate accounts. What was missing?
scenarios.situation: The user-provisioning script ran twice after a network retry and created 200 duplicate accounts. The script has no existence checks -- every run appends.
scenarios.title: Idempotent automation
scenarios.why: Automation runs in a world of retries, timeouts, and partial failures -- so every script must be safe to re-run: check state before acting, skip what exists, make operations convergent. Idempotency is not elegance; it is the difference between a retry and an incident. Logging records the duplicates; existence checks prevent them.

choices: Add an image-scan gate that fails the build on critical CVEs -- vulnerabilities should break the build, not ship
Scan but never fail -- developers hate red builds
Scan once a year -- enough for compliance
Only scan production images -- dev is safe
evidence: Last release shipped log4shell-equivalent in a base image; the scanner ran in advisory mode.
'Critical CVEs fail the build' was proposed and rejected as too strict.
scenarios.hint: When should a known-critical CVE stop a release?
scenarios.prompt: The scanner runs advisory-only; a critical CVE shipped. What changes?
scenarios.situation: Your pipeline scans container images in advisory mode. Last release shipped a critical CVE in a base image. A 'fail on critical' gate was previously rejected as too strict.
scenarios.title: Pipeline security gate
scenarios.why: Advisory scanning documents risk; gating prevents it. A fail-closed gate on critical CVEs (with a documented exception process for false positives and fix timelines) turns the scanner from a report into a control. 'Too strict' is negotiated via the exception process, not by shipping known-criticals. The gate belongs before the registry push -- after that, the vulnerability is distributed.

choices: Everyone commits to main and deploys from HEAD -- simplest
Long-lived feature branches per team -- isolation is safe
Trunk-based: short-lived branches, main always releasable, releases cut as tags -- with CI on every merge
No branches -- email patches around
evidence: Release 4.2 took 3 weeks to stabilize: 6 long-lived branches merged at once, conflicts everywhere.
Weekly releases with same-day hotfix ability.
scenarios.hint: What made 4.2 take 3 weeks?
scenarios.prompt: Six long-lived branches merged at once; release took 3 weeks. What workflow fixes this?
scenarios.situation: Release 4.2 took 3 weeks to stabilize after 6 long-lived branches merged simultaneously. The goal is weekly releases with same-day hotfix capability.
scenarios.title: Branching for releases
scenarios.why: Long-lived branches defer integration pain until release day -- then charge interest. Trunk-based development (short-lived branches, main always releasable, CI on every merge, releases as tags) integrates continuously so releases are a tagging decision, not a stabilization project. Hotfixes branch from the release tag, merge back to main. The 3 weeks were not bad luck; they were the workflow's invoice.

choices: Redeploy the old version manually -- 2 AM heroics build character
Blue-green or canary with automated health checks and one-command rollback -- reversibility is designed, not improvised
There is no rollback -- forward-fix only
Restore from backup tapes -- reliable and fast
evidence: Bad deploy at 2 AM; manual rollback took 90 minutes; the runbook was outdated.
scenarios.hint: The rollback took 6x the RTO. What was missing?
scenarios.prompt: Manual rollback took 90 minutes against a 15-minute RTO. What is the fix?
scenarios.situation: A bad 2 AM deploy took 90 minutes to roll back manually against a 15-minute RTO. The runbook was outdated; the engineer improvised.
scenarios.title: Rollback strategy
scenarios.why: Rollback is a design property, not a heroism opportunity: blue-green (two environments, instant switch) or canary (gradual traffic shift with automated health checks) make reversal a one-command, tested operation. Manual rollback under pressure with a stale runbook will always exceed the RTO. If you cannot roll back in minutes by design, you cannot meet the RTO -- fix the design, not the engineer.

choices: Alert on pipeline failure rate and duration -- the pipeline is production infrastructure
Check the pipeline when someone complains -- it usually works
Monitor only the app -- the pipeline is just tooling
Delete old pipeline runs to save disk -- hygiene is monitoring
evidence: Nobody noticed the nightly build failing for 6 days; Friday's release had no artifacts.
No alerts, no dashboard for pipeline health.
scenarios.hint: The release failed because the pipeline failed silently. What watches the watcher?
scenarios.prompt: Nightly builds failed silently for 6 days. What monitoring was missing?
scenarios.situation: The nightly build failed for 6 days unnoticed; Friday's release had no artifacts. There are no alerts and no dashboard for pipeline health.
scenarios.title: Pipeline health monitoring
scenarios.why: The pipeline is production infrastructure for your releases: alert on failure rate, duration anomalies, and artifact age, with a dashboard the team actually watches. Silent pipeline failures become release-day surprises -- the most expensive kind. 'It usually works' is not a monitoring strategy; it is a hope with a 6-day blind spot.

key_points: Generalist IT: networks, Windows/Linux, scripting, endpoints -- breadth with method.
Troubleshoot in layers: physical, network, DNS, app -- never skip.
Measure before acting: slow endpoints, full disks, failing services all get diagnosed first.
Backups are only real if restores are tested.
domains.name: Special Projects IT Engineer Track

choices: Reboot the server -- reboots fix most things
Isolate the layer: ping the IP, nslookup the name, tracert the path -- find which layer breaks
Reinstall the network driver -- drivers corrupt often
Replace the cable -- physical first, always
evidence: Ping 10.4.2.11 works. nslookup fileserver.corp.local fails. Tracert to the IP completes.
scenarios.hint: The IP works, the name does not. Which layer is that?
scenarios.prompt: IP reachable, name unresolvable. Where is the fault?
scenarios.situation: A workstation cannot reach fileserver.corp.local. Ping to 10.4.2.11 works, tracert completes, but nslookup of the name fails.
scenarios.title: Cannot reach the server
scenarios.why: Layer isolation: the network path works (ping/tracert to IP succeed), so this is a name-resolution failure, not a network failure. Rebooting, reinstalling drivers, or replacing cables treats the wrong layer. Check DNS client config, the DNS server, and the record -- the tests already told you where to look.

choices: Reinstall the application -- fastest fix
Start the service repeatedly until it holds
Check dependencies and the event log: which dependency failed, what did the System/Application log record at the failure time
Disable the firewall -- services hate firewalls
evidence: Print spooler service stops 30 seconds after every manual start.
Event Viewer: 'The Print Spooler service terminated unexpectedly' preceded by a faulty printer driver load error.
scenarios.hint: The log names the cause. What is the method?
scenarios.prompt: A Windows service dies 30 seconds after every start. What is the method?
scenarios.situation: The print spooler stops 30 seconds after each manual start. Event Viewer shows the termination preceded by a faulty printer driver load error.
scenarios.title: Windows service will not start
scenarios.why: Services fail for reasons, and Windows logs them: check the service's dependencies first, then the event log around the failure timestamp. Here the log names a faulty driver -- the fix is the driver, not the service. Reinstalling the app or hammering 'start' treats symptoms; the event log is the diagnosis.

choices: Get-ChildItem -Recurse | Sort-Object Length -Descending | Select-Object -First 10 FullName, Length
dir /s -- then eyeball it
Delete temp files first -- that is always the cause
Reboot -- disk issues are transient
evidence: Find the 10 largest files on the E: drive, full paths and sizes.
Must be a one-liner the tech can paste.
scenarios.hint: Recurse, sort by size descending, take 10.
scenarios.prompt: Find the 10 largest files on E: as a one-liner.
scenarios.situation: A tech needs the 10 largest files on E: with full paths and sizes, as a paste-ready PowerShell one-liner.
scenarios.title: PowerShell: largest files
scenarios.why: Get-ChildItem -Recurse enumerates, Sort-Object Length -Descending orders by size, Select-Object -First 10 takes the top with the needed properties. One pipeline, no eyeballing, no destructive guessing. The general pattern -- enumerate, sort, select -- answers half of all admin 'find the big X' questions.

choices: Delete the largest files immediately -- space is space
Find what is consuming: df for filesystems, du for directories, check logrotate -- then act on the cause
Add a bigger disk -- hardware solves software problems
Reboot -- full disks are transient
evidence: /var/log is 80% of usage; one application's log was never rotated.
scenarios.hint: What is consuming the space -- and why did it grow unbounded?
scenarios.prompt: Root filesystem 100% full. What is the discipline?
scenarios.situation: A Linux server's root filesystem is full. du shows /var/log at 80% of usage -- one application's log was never rotated.
scenarios.title: Linux disk full
scenarios.why: Diagnose before deleting: df identifies the filesystem, du identifies the consumer, and the cause here is a missing logrotate config -- deleting the log without fixing rotation just schedules the next outage. The discipline is find-the-consumer, fix-the-cause (logrotate), then reclaim. Deleting blindly risks the wrong files; adding disk funds the leak.

choices: Assign static IPs to everything -- deterministic
Extend the existing DHCP scope -- bigger is better
Configure DHCP relay (IP helper) on the new VLAN's router interface pointing at the DHCP server, with a scope for the new subnet
Disable DHCP -- static is more secure
evidence: New VLAN 40, subnet 10.40.0.0/24. DHCP server lives on VLAN 10.
Clients on VLAN 40 get no addresses; DHCPDISCOVER never reaches the server.
scenarios.hint: DHCPDISCOVER is a broadcast. What stops broadcasts at the VLAN boundary?
scenarios.prompt: New VLAN, no DHCP leases. What is missing?
scenarios.situation: VLAN 40 (10.40.0.0/24) is live but clients get no DHCP leases. The DHCP server sits on VLAN 10; DHCPDISCOVER broadcasts never cross the VLAN boundary.
scenarios.title: DHCP for the new VLAN
scenarios.why: DHCP discovery is broadcast-based and broadcasts do not cross VLANs -- the relay (IP helper) on VLAN 40's router interface forwards the discovers to the server as unicast, and a matching scope serves the new subnet. Static addressing 'works' at the cost of every future change; extending the old scope serves the wrong subnet. The helper address is the standard answer.

choices: Run gpresult /r, check scope/security filtering, verify replication between DCs -- scope, filtering, replication, in that order
Reinstall the printer -- drivers fix policy
Reboot the DC -- replication needs encouragement
Delete and recreate the GPO -- faster than debugging
evidence: Printer-deployment GPO applies to half the OU's workstations.
gpresult on a failing host: 'Filtering: Denied (Security)' -- the computer account is not in the filtered group.
scenarios.hint: Half work, half do not. What differs between the halves?
scenarios.prompt: GPO applies to half the OU. What is the order of operations?
scenarios.situation: A printer-deployment GPO reaches half the workstations in its OU. gpresult on a failing host shows 'Filtering: Denied (Security)' -- the computer account is not in the security-filtered group.
scenarios.title: GPO not applying
scenarios.why: Group Policy troubleshooting is scope-first: gpresult reveals scope and filtering, and here security filtering excluded the failing half -- the fix is group membership, not the GPO. Replication and enforcement come next in the order. Reinstalling printers or rebuilding the GPO burns the session; the scope answer was in gpresult all along.

choices: Open the 2 GB log in Notepad -- visual inspection
grep 'ERROR' app.log | awk '{print $1, $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -20 -- errors by hour, ranked
Restart the app -- logs are history
Email the log to the vendor -- let them read it
evidence: Top error signatures by hour from a 2 GB application log.
Each line starts with a timestamp; the 5th field is the error code.
scenarios.hint: Filter, extract, count, rank -- the pipeline pattern.
scenarios.prompt: Top error signatures by hour from a 2 GB log. What is the pipeline?
scenarios.situation: You need the top error signatures by hour from a 2 GB application log. Lines start with timestamps; the 5th field is the error code.
scenarios.title: Bash: parse the logs
scenarios.why: The filter-extract-count-rank pipeline: grep isolates ERROR lines, awk pulls hour and code, sort | uniq -c counts, sort -rn ranks, head takes the top 20. It answers the question in seconds on 2 GB without opening anything. Visual inspection does not scale; restarting destroys the evidence; the vendor does not need your log.

choices: Reimage it -- fastest resolution
Add more RAM -- slowness is always RAM
Measure first: Resource Monitor for the bottleneck (CPU/disk/RAM), startup impact, AV scan state -- then act on the data
Defrag the SSD -- fragmentation slows everything
evidence: 'My laptop is unbearably slow.' No specifics.
Resource Monitor: disk at 100% active time, AV full scan running, 40 startup items.
scenarios.hint: Three candidate causes, one measurement. What does the data say?
scenarios.prompt: 'Unbearably slow' laptop. What is the triage order?
scenarios.situation: A user reports an unbearably slow laptop with no specifics. Resource Monitor shows disk at 100% active time with an AV full scan running and 40 startup items.
scenarios.title: Endpoint slow
scenarios.why: Measure before acting: Resource Monitor identifies the actual bottleneck (disk saturation from the AV scan plus startup bloat), which beats guessing at RAM or reimaging. The fix follows the data -- reschedule the scan, trim startup, then re-measure. Reimaging 'works' at the cost of the user's day; defragging an SSD does nothing. Triage is measurement, then action.

choices: Verify with test restores: regularly restore to an isolated target and confirm the data -- untested backups are hopes, not backups
Check the 'backup succeeded' emails -- green means good
Trust the software -- it is enterprise-grade
Count the tapes -- inventory is verification
evidence: Backups report success nightly for 8 months.
First-ever restore test: 30% of archives fail integrity checks.
scenarios.hint: What does 'backup succeeded' actually prove?
scenarios.prompt: 8 months of green backup reports; first restore test fails 30%. What was missing?
scenarios.situation: Backups reported success nightly for 8 months. The first-ever restore test reveals 30% of archives fail integrity checks.
scenarios.title: Backup verification
scenarios.why: 'Backup succeeded' proves the job ran, not that the data is recoverable -- only test restores prove that. Regular restore drills to an isolated target, with integrity checks, are the actual control; everything else is a hope with a green dashboard. The 8 months of green reports measured the wrong thing. Verify recovery, not completion.
